Before You Read What This Book Is This book tells the story of SpaceX, the rocket company that changed what the world thinks is possible in space. It follows the company from a small group of engineers in a California warehouse to the operator of the busiest launch fleet on Earth. It explains, in plain language, how rockets work, why reusing them matters, how a satellite internet network functions, and what the giant Starship rocket is meant to do. It is written for curious readers, students, and anyone who wants to understand a company they hear about every week without needing an engineering degree.

What This Book Is Not This is an independent book. It is not authorized, endorsed, or sponsored by SpaceX or any person named in it. It does not contain secret information. Everything here comes from public sources: company statements, government reports, news coverage, court and regulatory records, and the long history of spaceflight. Where a claim comes from the company or from its critics, the book says so.

How to Read It ◆ The chapters run roughly in time order, but each can be read alone. ◆ Gold boxes mark ideas worth remembering or cautions worth noticing. ◆ Diagrams are drawn for this book to show how things work.

◆ At the back is a workbook, a glossary, a timeline, and discussion questions.

A Note on Numbers Numbers about launches, valuations, and satellites change quickly. This book uses figures reported in public sources through autumn 2026. Treat every number as a snapshot, and check current sources before you rely on it. THE RULE OF THIS BOOK

Admire what was achieved, question what is claimed, and always ask who benefits from the story being told.

PART ONE

Dream and Near-Death

CHAPTER 1

Why Start a Rocket Company? The Question That Started It In the early 2000s, after selling his stake in PayPal, Elon Musk was a very wealthy young man with a question that struck many friends as odd: why had humanity stopped going to the Moon? Apollo had ended in 1972. Thirty years later, no human had traveled beyond low Earth orbit. NASA's budget was a small fraction of what it had been at the height of the space race, and the Space Shuttle, supposed to make spaceflight routine, was expensive, aging, and had suffered the loss of Challenger in 1986 and Columbia in 2003. Musk has said that he first imagined a small philanthropic project rather than a company. He thought about sending a greenhouse to Mars, a plant growing on the red planet, to reignite public excitement. The idea, sometimes called Mars Oasis, was meant to inspire a new generation, in the way that Apollo had.

The Trip to Russia To find a rocket to carry the greenhouse, Musk traveled to Russia in 2001 and 2002, accompanied by friends such as Jim Cantrell, a space-industry consultant, and Adeo Ressi. They hoped to buy a refurbished intercontinental ballistic missile. Accounts of the meetings, including those in Ashlee Vance's biography

and in Eric Berger's history of the company, describe tense, sometimes insulting negotiations. The Russians reportedly quoted prices that Musk considered absurd, and on the flight home he is said to have concluded that if the price was the problem, he could build the rocket himself. On that return flight, Musk reportedly built a spreadsheet to find out how much it would cost to make a rocket from raw materials. The conclusion was that the cost of materials was a small share of the price that rocket buyers paid. If that was right, the industry's high prices came from how rockets were built and sold, not from physics. FIRST PRINCIPLES IN ACTION

This is the story most often told about Musk's "first principles" approach: ask what a thing is made of and what those materials cost, then ask why the price is so much higher. It is an effective question, but it can also mislead. The cost of materials is not the cost of engineering, testing, and reliability. SpaceX's early years would show how much work lay between the spreadsheet and a working rocket.

Founding the Company Space Exploration Technologies Corp., known as SpaceX, was founded in June 2002. Musk invested about $100 million of his own money, a large part of what he had received from the sale of PayPal. The company's first home was a rented warehouse in El Segundo, California, near Los Angeles International Airport. The first employees were few: a handful of engineers recruited from established aerospace companies and from Musk's network. Among the most important early hires were: ◆ Tom Mueller, a propulsion engineer who had built rocket engines as a hobby

and worked at TRW. He became the company's chief propulsion engineer and

led the design of the Merlin engine. ◆ Gwynne Shotwell, who joined in 2002 as vice president of business

development, became president in 2008 and has led the company's operations and customer relations since. ◆ Hans Koenigsmann, a German engineer who became a key voice on flight

reliability. ◆ Chris Thompson, Tim Buzza, Jeremy Hollman and others who built the

first vehicles and tests.

The Business Idea The business idea had three parts. 1. Build small, cheap rockets first. The company would start with a small

launcher, the Falcon 1, to prove that a small team could reach orbit. 2. Make as much as possible in-house. Building parts internally would let the

company control cost, schedule, and quality. 3. Aim for reuse. From early on, Musk argued that making rockets reusable was

the only way to make spaceflight truly cheap. A fully reusable rocket, he liked to say, would be like an airline that threw away the plane after every flight. None of these ideas was entirely new. Others had proposed reusable rockets, and some in the industry had experimented with them. What was unusual was a founder willing to spend his own money and to stay with the idea through repeated failure.

The Skeptics Conventional wisdom in the industry in 2002 was that a new company could not break in. The launch market was dominated by Boeing and Lockheed Martin,

which had combined their launch operations as United Launch Alliance in 2006, and by European and Russian providers. Government customers preferred proven vehicles. Insurance costs for a new launcher were high. The history of start-up rocket companies was grim: many had tried, and almost all had folded. Several people close to the project reportedly advised Musk to put the money elsewhere. He later said that he gave the company a small chance of success, perhaps ten percent, and invested anyway, because he felt the goal was important.

What the Early Years Tell Us The founding of SpaceX shows traits that recur in the story: impatience with the way things are done, willingness to risk personal money, and a talent for recruiting people who believe in the mission. It also shows how much the success of the company would rest on others: the engineers who built the hardware, the customers who gave contracts, and the government agencies that would later provide the money to keep the company alive. CHAPTER 2

A Short History of Spaceflight SpaceX arrived in a field with a long and dramatic history. Knowing the background makes its achievements, and its limits, much easier to judge.

The First Race On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. The shock in the United States was immense, and within a year Congress had created NASA. On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and a few weeks later Alan Shepard became the first American. In May 1961 President John F. Kennedy committed the nation to landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out.

Apollo NASA's Apollo program built the Saturn V rocket, still the most massive rocket to have flown successfully before Starship, standing about 111 meters tall. Apollo 8 carried astronauts around the Moon in December 1968. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon in Apollo 11. Six lunar landings followed, ending with Apollo 17 in December 1972. The program took a large share of the federal budget at its peak, and political support faded once the goal had been reached.

The Space Shuttle The Space Shuttle, which flew from 1981 to 2011, was conceived as a reusable spaceplane that would make flights cheap and frequent. In practice it needed extensive refurbishment between flights, and costs per launch were far higher than promised. The program flew 135 missions, built much of the International Space Station, and launched the Hubble Space Telescope. It also suffered two fatal accidents: Challenger, which broke apart 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986, and Columbia, which disintegrated on reentry on February 1, 2003. Both accidents killed all seven crew members aboard and were investigated in detail, with findings that pointed to organizational as well as technical failures. The Shuttle left a bitter lesson about reusability: reusing hardware does not save money if inspecting and repairing it costs nearly as much as building new.

The Quiet Decades After Apollo, human spaceflight stayed in low Earth orbit. Robotic probes explored the planets: Voyager, Viking, Mars rovers, Cassini, and many others. Launching satellites became a business of large government contractors working under cost-plus contracts, where the government pays costs plus a fee. Such contracts reward spending, not saving. Prices per launch remained high, and few expected a change.

The Spark of Commercial Space Several developments in the 1990s and early 2000s opened the door to private companies. ◆ DC-X. In the early 1990s a small experimental vehicle called the Delta

Clipper flew short vertical-takeoff-and-landing hops in New Mexico, showing that a rocket could land on its tail. The program ended after an accident in

1996 but inspired a generation of engineers. ◆ The Ansari X Prize. A $10 million prize for the first private craft to reach

space twice in two weeks was won on October 4, 2004, by Burt Rutan's SpaceShipOne, backed by Paul Allen. Though suborbital, it showed that private companies could fly humans to space. ◆ NASA's commercial programs. After the Columbia accident, NASA

decided to retire the Shuttle and rely on private companies for cargo and crew transport to the station. Its Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program, begun in 2006, used fixed-price payments for milestones in place of cost-plus contracts. SpaceX was one of the winners.

Where SpaceX Fits SpaceX built on these precedents: vertical landing as shown by DC-X, the commercial opening created by NASA's policy, and decades of rocket engineering in the open literature. Its contribution was to execute at scale, to drive down costs through reuse, and to build a business that did not depend on a single customer. The result changed the industry, but it was a development, not a creation from nothing. CREDIT WHERE IT IS DUE

Every success in this book rests on earlier work by scientists, engineers, and policymakers. A healthy account of any innovator acknowledges the shoulders on which they stand.

CHAPTER 3

How Rockets Really Work: A Plain-English Tour The Parts of a Rocket Every orbital rocket, whatever its size, has the same basic parts. ◆ Propellant tanks. Most of a rocket is tanks. In a Falcon 9 first stage, there are

tanks for kerosene and for liquid oxygen. ◆ Engines. Pumps push propellant into a combustion chamber, where it burns

and the hot gas rushes out of a nozzle. ◆ Structure. The skin and frames hold everything together and must be strong

yet light. ◆ Guidance and control. Computers, sensors, and moving engines or fins steer

the vehicle. ◆ Payload. A satellite, capsule, or cargo, protected on top by a fairing.

Inside an Engine A rocket engine is surprisingly simple in idea: burn fuel with an oxidizer and let the exhaust leave through a nozzle. The difficulty is in the details. The combustion chamber operates at temperatures that would melt most metals, so the

fuel is often circulated around the chamber walls to cool it first. Turbopumps spin tens of thousands of times a minute to push propellants in against high pressure. A turbopump on a large engine can deliver as much power as a locomotive in a package the size of a desk.

Why Landing Is Hard A landing booster must slow from several hundred meters per second to zero with an engine that cannot throttle below a certain level. The engine is so powerful relative to the nearly empty rocket that it cannot hover; it can only come to a stop at exactly the right moment. Engineers call this a "hoverslam" or "suicide burn": the burn must start at exactly the right altitude and end just as the legs touch. Start too early and the rocket stops and climbs; too late and it hits the ground.

Steering Rockets steer by moving their engines (gimbaling), using small thrusters, or using grid fins, which are flat lattices that act as rudders in the air. Falcon boosters use four titanium grid fins, which fold flat during ascent and swing out during descent.

Safety Systems Rockets carry flight termination systems that can destroy them if they veer toward populated areas. Range safety officers or automatic systems decide. SpaceX has moved to an autonomous system on Falcon, which reduces the number of people and equipment needed on the range and speeds up launches.

Why Rocket Fuel Choices Matter ◆ Kerosene (RP-1) is dense and easy to handle, but it leaves soot, which can

matter for reuse. ◆ Liquid hydrogen is very efficient but light and hard to store; it needs huge

tanks. ◆ Methane is a middle choice, clean, reasonably dense, and potentially

makeable on Mars. ◆ Solid propellant is simple and stores well but cannot be turned off once lit. ◆ Hypergolic fuels ignite on contact and are used in thrusters; they are toxic.

CHAPTER 4

Kwajalein and the Falcon 1 A Rocket for a Small Company The Falcon 1 was designed to be small. It was a two-stage rocket, about 21 meters tall, powered on its first stage by a single Merlin engine burning kerosene and liquid oxygen. It could carry a few hundred kilograms to low orbit, small enough to compete with the cheapest launchers and large enough, SpaceX hoped, to serve small satellite customers. More importantly, it was a proving ground. Every system, from engines to avionics to launch operations, would have to work for the company to move on to bigger rockets. The Merlin engine, designed by Tom Mueller's team, used a pintle injector, a design lineage that traced back to the engine on the Apollo lunar module. The first-stage engine used an ablative nozzle that burned away in a controlled manner to protect itself from heat. The company tested engines in the Texas desert, at a former airfield and test site near McGregor, which would grow into its main rocket-testing center.

Why an Island in the Pacific? Launching a rocket requires open space for safety. SpaceX chose the Reagan Test Site on Omelek Island, part of the Kwajalein Atoll in the Marshall Islands. The

U.S. Army ran a missile test range there, and the atoll's position near the equator gave a launch boost from the Earth's rotation. It was also about as far from a factory as it was possible to be. Crews had to ship rockets by sea and air, live on a remote island, and manage logistics across thousands of miles of ocean. Engineers have described the launch campaigns as grueling, with heat, salt air that corroded equipment, and long days. The sea air was a particular problem: salt and moisture got into everything. Many of the lessons about preparation, redundancy, and checklists were learned there.

Failure One: March 2006 The first launch attempt took place on March 24, 2006. The Falcon 1 lifted off, but about half a minute into the flight an engine fire developed. The fire damaged the vehicle and the first stage shut down, and the rocket fell back near the pad. The investigation traced the failure to a corroded aluminum nut in the fuel system, damaged by the salt air of the island. It was a small part, and it had destroyed a rocket. The lesson was bitter and simple: a flight-critical part had been left to chance. SpaceX changed its materials and its inspection procedures. The payload that was lost was a small satellite built by the U.S. Air Force Academy.

Failure Two: March 2007 Almost a year later, on March 21, 2007, the second Falcon 1 flew much further. The first stage worked, stage separation succeeded, and the second stage ignited. But a problem developed with the second stage, in which fuel sloshing, caused by the rocket's rotation, produced a pitch oscillation. The rocket began to roll, and the stage shut down before it could reach orbit. The launch got to space, at about 289 kilometers up, but not into orbit. The company called the flight a partial

success, since much of the new vehicle had worked, and it gathered the data it needed to fix the problem.

Failure Three: August 2008 The third attempt, on August 2, 2008, was the one that threatened the company's survival. The first stage burned well and separated, but on separation the first-stage engine, still producing residual thrust, bumped the second stage. The rocket had a new, more powerful first-stage engine design, with a regeneratively cooled engine, and the residual thrust was higher than the models predicted. The stages collided, and the mission was lost. It carried small payloads including a NASA experiment and ashes of several people, including actor James Doohan of Star Trek. By then SpaceX had spent most of its money. Three failed launches, a strained relationship with early customers, and the 2008 financial crisis put the company, and Musk's other business Tesla, on the edge.

Success: September 2008 On September 28, 2008, the fourth Falcon 1 flew. It carried a mass simulator and no real satellite, because the company's leadership had decided that it would not risk a customer's payload again. The first stage burned, the stages separated cleanly this time, the second stage ignited and reached orbit. It was the first privately developed liquid-fueled rocket to reach Earth orbit. Musk has said that if the fourth launch had failed, he would have had no money to try a fifth. In July 2009 the Falcon 1 flew its fifth and last mission, carrying the Malaysian RazakSAT satellite, the first commercial payload to reach orbit on a SpaceX rocket. The vehicle was then retired in favor of the larger Falcon 9.

CHAPTER 5

The Money Runs Out Christmas 2008 The last weeks of 2008 are the most dramatic in the history of both SpaceX and Tesla. Musk's personal fortune had been spread across the two companies. Tesla was in a cash crisis, with the financial system seized up and car sales collapsing. SpaceX had one successful flight after three failures, and it had spent heavily. Both companies were close to running out of money. On December 23, 2008, NASA announced the award of Commercial Resupply Services contracts. SpaceX was selected to deliver cargo to the International Space Station in a contract worth about $1.6 billion for a minimum of twelve flights. Musk has said that he received the call from NASA when he was on the verge of losing the company, and that his reaction was to say that he loved NASA. The contract covered the development of the Falcon 9 rocket and the Dragon capsule and gave SpaceX a customer, and a payment schedule, that could carry it for years. That same week, Tesla closed a financing round that kept it alive. Within a few days, both companies had been saved.

Why NASA Took the Chance NASA's decision was not an act of charity. The agency had a problem. The Space Shuttle was scheduled to retire after the Columbia accident review, and after 2011 the United States would have no way to carry cargo, or crews, to the International Space Station except by buying seats on Russian Soyuz spacecraft or relying on partners. The agency's leaders, notably Mike Griffin, who was NASA Administrator from 2005 to 2009, and Scott Horowitz, along with Alan Lindenmoyer who managed the commercial program, wanted to create a commercial market for such services. The method was a new kind of contract. Under traditional "cost-plus" contracts, a company was paid its costs and a fee, which gave little incentive to be efficient. Under COTS, the Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program started in 2006, NASA paid fixed amounts when a company reached defined milestones, and the company kept the risk of overruns. SpaceX won COTS funding of roughly $278 million in 2006, later increased, and the CRS contract was the follow-on to deliver cargo. Estimates of NASA's cost savings differ, but a 2011 NASA analysis of the Falcon 9's development, using a standard cost model, estimated that the cost of a conventional government approach would have been several times higher than what SpaceX actually spent, about $390 million for Falcon 9 versus an estimated $1.7 to 4 billion. The finding was widely cited, and it was also debated, since NASA's model can only approximate what a different approach might have cost. LESSON: THE GOVERNMENT AS A CUSTOMER

SpaceX's early survival rested on a government agency that chose to buy services rather than own rockets. This was a policy decision made by officials, and it is as much a part of the story as the engineering. Without COTS, the company might not have lived.

Other Backers Money also came from private investors. After the first Falcon 1 failures, Founders Fund, the venture firm of Peter Thiel and others, invested in 2008, a significant vote of confidence when few others would. Draper Fisher Jurvetson was another early investor. Musk himself put in much of his remaining money, famously borrowing from friends to pay his own rent during the worst of 2008.

The Pace of Hiring By 2009, SpaceX had grown to more than a thousand employees. Many came from universities and from established companies, drawn by the chance to work on real flight hardware early in their careers. The company was known for a culture of long hours, direct communication, and decisions made by engineers close to the problem, rather than by layers of management.

What the Near-Death Taught the Company ◆ Never put all risk on one launch. After 2008, SpaceX built backup plans for

its manifest and customers. ◆ Customers matter. Contracts from NASA and later from commercial

satellite operators allowed the company to fund development of new rockets. ◆ Cash is a weapon. Having a cushion of cash meant the company could

Case Files: Failures and What They Taught Engineering progress is often a story of failure studied honestly. This chapter walks through notable failures, mostly from SpaceX and also from earlier programs, and asks what each one teaches.

Case 1: Falcon 1 Flight 1 (March 2006) About half a minute after liftoff from Kwajalein, a fuel leak caused a fire, and the engine failed. The team moved to stainless steel hardware and revised handling procedures.

The lesson was that fluid dynamics inside tanks can matter as much as engine thrust. The team added baffles and improved control software.

Case 3: Falcon 1 Flight 3 (August 2008) The first stage's engine continued to push briefly after stage separation, bumping the second stage. A change to a newer engine type with residual thrust had not been fully accounted for in the timing. The lesson was that a change that looks safe can break assumptions elsewhere. It was a painful flight for a company running out of money.

Case 4: Falcon 9 CRS-7 (June 2015) A Falcon 9 carrying a Dragon cargo capsule to the station broke apart about two minutes into flight. The investigation found that a strut holding a helium bottle inside the second-stage oxygen tank failed, probably because of a flaw in the part's material or its use at load beyond its rating. SpaceX changed its testing and inspection of such components, and the Dragon's parachutes were later modified so a capsule can survive a rocket failure if software allows.

Case 5: The Amos-6 Pad Explosion (September 2016) During preparation for a routine static-fire test, a Falcon 9 exploded on the pad, destroying the rocket and a satellite worth about $200 million. The cause, after months of study, was found to be a combination of factors: buckled composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs) inside the oxygen tank, and a process of loading very cold oxygen that created pockets of solid oxygen between the carbon fiber and liner, which ignited by friction. Case 6: Starship SN8 (December 2020) The prototype flew to roughly 12.5 kilometers, performed its belly-flop maneuver, and flipped upright, but its landing burn failed because of low pressure in a fuel tank, and the vehicle hit the pad and exploded. Musk called the test a success in terms of data, which became typical language for the program. The accident led to redesigned hatches, fewer flammable materials, and a different atmosphere for launch. The lesson is that testing on the ground is dangerous too.

Myths and Facts Myth: Rockets are just big firecrackers Fact: Solid rockets are similar in principle, but liquid-fueled rockets are among the most complex machines made, with turbopumps, cryogenic plumbing, and precise computers.

Myth: There is no gravity in space Fact: Gravity at the station's altitude is about 90 percent of what it is at the surface. Astronauts float because they are in continuous free fall around Earth.

Myth: Reusable rockets are obviously cheaper Fact: Reuse saves only if refurbishment costs less than building new and the rocket flies enough times. The Space Shuttle showed that reuse can be expensive.

Myth: SpaceX invented reusable rockets Fact: The idea is old, and earlier programs such as the Shuttle and DC-X explored it. Blue Origin landed a suborbital booster before SpaceX landed an orbital one. SpaceX's achievement was making orbital reuse routine.

Myth: SpaceX gets handouts and does nothing without NASA Fact: NASA is a major customer and has paid for development milestones, but SpaceX also invested its own money, and it wins commercial and national security business. The truth is a partnership, with both public and private money.

Myth: Starlink satellites will make space unusable Fact: The risks of debris and congestion are real and being studied, but the satellites are in low orbits where dead ones fall within a few years. The concern is serious but not the same as certainty of disaster.

Myth: Everything said by the company's leader comes true Fact: Many of his goals have been achieved, and many dates have slipped by years. Check each claim against the record.

Myth: Everything said against the company is false Fact: Critics have raised real concerns about safety, the environment, labor, and concentration of power. Some criticisms are exaggerated; some are well-founded.

Myth: Mars is the next Earth Fact: Mars has a thin atmosphere, extreme cold, high radiation, and toxic soil. Living there would be harder than living in Antarctica or at the bottom of the ocean.

Myth: Astronauts are weightless because they are far from Earth Fact: See above. The station is only 400 kilometers up, closer than many cities are to each other.

Myth: Space is silent and empty Fact: Space has no air to carry sound, but it holds radiation, tiny particles, and plasma. Inside a spacecraft, there is plenty of noise from fans and pumps.

Myth: You can see the Great Wall from space Fact: It is hard to see with the naked eye from orbit. Cities at night are far easier to spot.

Light travels faster in a vacuum than through glass fiber, so a laser path in space can be faster than an undersea cable over long distances.

Orbital Refueling and Why Starship Needs It The Rocket Equation A rocket's power is limited by a simple relationship: to go faster, you need more fuel, but more fuel is itself weight that needs more fuel to lift. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation shows that the mass of fuel grows exponentially with the speed change needed. This is why reaching the Moon or Mars is so costly.

The Gas Station in Orbit Starship is designed so that after reaching Earth orbit, it can be refueled by additional Starships called tankers. A single Starship in orbit with empty tanks has little ability to go to the Moon or Mars; full tanks give it enough. The plan requires several tanker flights for each deep-space mission, the number depending on design details that have changed over time. The technology is not trivial. Propellants are cryogenic: liquid oxygen at about minus 183 degrees Celsius and liquid methane at about minus 162 degrees Celsius. In microgravity, liquids float and do not settle at the bottom of a tank, so pumps need a way to collect them. Transfer between two vehicles requires docking, pressure control, and avoiding boil-off from sunlight. Small-scale

demonstrations have been done with other systems, but nothing at the scale needed. NASA and SpaceX have discussed ship-to-ship transfer demonstrations as milestones.

It would need to be refueled in Earth orbit before heading to the Moon. This makes orbital refueling a critical path item, and a delay there affects the schedule of the whole program.

The Physics Behind the Rocket This chapter explains, in plain language, the science that every chapter of this book relies on. No math beyond arithmetic is needed.

Newton's Three Laws 1. An object stays at rest or moves in a straight line unless a force acts. A

rocket in empty space keeps its speed. 2. Force equals mass times acceleration. A heavier rocket needs more thrust to

speed up at the same rate. 3. For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. A rocket pushes

hot gas downward, and the gas pushes the rocket upward. It does not need air to push against.

Orbit Is Falling Sideways Imagine firing a cannonball horizontally from a high mountain. With more speed, it lands farther away. At about 7.8 kilometers per second near Earth's surface, the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls, so it never lands. That is orbit. Astronauts float because they and the spacecraft are in continuous free fall, not because there is no gravity. Gravity at the height of the space station is about 90 percent as strong as on the ground.

Why It Takes So Much Fuel Getting to orbit takes much more sideways speed than height. The International Space Station is only about 400 kilometers up, a distance you could drive in a few hours, but it travels at about 28,000 kilometers per hour. Building It: The Technology Deep Dives Stainless Steel Starship's decision to use stainless steel in place of carbon fiber surprised many. Carbon fiber is lighter, but it is expensive, slow to produce, and weakens at high temperatures. Stainless steel in the 300 series is cheap, easy to weld, and gets stronger at cryogenic temperatures. At reentry temperatures it holds up well, so the windward side needs a lighter heat shield than a carbon-fiber ship would. The steel has a total mass cost, but the process speed more than makes up for it, according to the company's reasoning. Time will tell whether the full system meets its goals.

Friction Stir Welding Falcon's tanks are made of aluminum-lithium alloy joined by friction stir welding. A rotating tool presses into the seam and heats the metal until it becomes plastic and mixes, without melting. The result is a joint stronger than a conventional weld. The technique was developed in the 1990s at The Welding Institute in Britain and is now used in aerospace and shipbuilding.

3D Printing SpaceX prints parts such as engine components in metal. Dragon's SuperDraco engine chamber is printed from a nickel-chromium superalloy, an early example of flight-critical 3D-printed hardware. Printing enables complex internal passages for cooling and reduces the number of parts.

Avionics and Software Falcon uses commercial processors in triplicate, comparing their outputs to reject faults, rather than using older, slower radiation-hardened chips. The flight software runs on Linux with custom code written in C++. Engineers say the philosophy is to use ordinary hardware, and to tolerate faults with redundancy. The approach reduces cost and improves performance but needs careful testing.

Grid Fins and Cold Gas Thrusters Grid fins give a booster control in the air. On later Falcons these are titanium for heat tolerance. Cold gas thrusters (compressed nitrogen) flip the booster after stage separation, and they use no complicated fuel. The simple solution is a reminder of engineering's trade-off between elegance and reliability.

Autonomous Landing A booster's computer decides its own landing path using inertial sensors, GPS, and radar. It computes a new trajectory many times per second with software that solves an optimization problem in real time. Researchers, including Lars Blackmore, who worked at SpaceX, developed the math, called convex optimization, to make this tractable on flight computers.

Thermal Protection Dragon capsules use a heat shield material called PICA-X, a variant of NASA's phenolic impregnated carbon ablator developed by SpaceX. It chars and erodes in a controlled way, carrying heat away. Starship's tiles are made of silica and designed for reuse.

traditional programs. ◆ Data review after every flight, with anomalies logged and tracked.

Vertical integration reduces markups and shortens iteration loops, but it requires large facilities and workforce. Critics note that in-house parts may hide costs that a supplier might manage better. A Student's Guide: Math, Models, and Projects The Math You Need This book needs only arithmetic, but the real work of rocketry uses algebra, calculus, and physics. A short tour of the key ideas follows. Speed, Distance, and Time

Speed equals distance divided by time. A satellite at 7.6 kilometers per second covers 456 kilometers in a minute. At that speed, an orbit around Earth, about 40,000 kilometers at that height, takes roughly 90 minutes. Mass Ratio

If a rocket weighs 100 tons at liftoff and 10 tons when empty, its mass ratio is 10. Higher ratios give more speed. The Rocket Equation, Without Fear

The change in speed equals the exhaust speed times the natural logarithm of the mass ratio. A natural log is just a button on a calculator. Example: with exhaust speed of 3 kilometers per second and a mass ratio of 10, the natural log of 10 is about 2.3, so the speed gain is about 6.9 kilometers per second. To reach orbit, we need around 9.4 kilometers per second including losses, so a single stage is not

enough with that exhaust speed, which is why we use stages. Cost per Kilogram

Divide the launch price by the mass delivered. If a launch sells for $70 million and carries 17,500 kilograms to low orbit, the cost is $4,000 per kilogram. The Shuttle was often estimated at tens of thousands of dollars per kilogram. Rounding and Error

Be careful with estimates. Always record units and sources, and say whether a number is a measurement, a forecast, or a rough guess.

Pioneers Beyond SpaceX Rocketry is the work of generations. Meeting some of the people before and beside SpaceX helps put the company in context.

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky (1857 to 1935) A deaf Russian schoolteacher, he derived the rocket equation in 1903 and imagined space stations and multistage rockets. He wrote that Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in a cradle forever.

Robert Goddard (1882 to 1945) An American physicist who launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926, in Auburn, Massachusetts. It flew for about two and a half seconds. Goddard patented key ideas, including multistage rockets and gyroscopic guidance. The press mocked his belief that rockets could work in a vacuum, and a correction came decades later, after Apollo 11.

Wernher von Braun (1912 to 1977) A German engineer who led V-2 rocket development during World War II. The V-2 was built using forced labor, and thousands of prisoners died in its production. After the war, the United States brought him and other engineers to

the country through Operation Paperclip. He led the team that developed the Saturn V. His career raises moral questions about science and responsibility.

Sergei Korolev (1907 to 1966) The chief designer of the Soviet space program, he led the launches of Sputnik and Gagarin. He survived the Gulag and worked in secret, unknown to the public until his death.

Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan, and Mary Jackson Black women mathematicians and engineers at NASA, whose work was essential to early American spaceflight, and whose story was told in the book and film Hidden Figures. Johnson calculated trajectories for Alan Shepard's flight and checked computer results for John Glenn's orbit.

Gene Kranz The flight director who led the Apollo 13 rescue, famous for the principle that failure is not an option, a line from the movie more than a quote from him. His team improvised a way to bring the crew home after an oxygen tank exploded.

Burt Rutan An aircraft designer whose SpaceShipOne won the Ansari X Prize. His designs showed that small teams could do what governments had only done before.

Ten Big Debates These are open questions about space. Reasonable people disagree on each, and your best answer is the one you can defend with evidence.

1. Should humans or robots explore? Robots are cheaper, tougher, and expendable. Humans adapt and discover quickly. A combination may be best.

2. Is Mars the right goal? Some say the Moon, or orbiting stations, or asteroids should come first. Others say Mars is the horizon that inspires.

3. Should private companies lead? Commercial competition drives cost down. Government has a duty of public interest, safety, and long-term science. A mix of both is common.

4. Who sets the rules in orbit? International treaties are old and vague. National laws vary. New rules may be needed for traffic management, debris, and resources.

5. Can mega-constellations coexist with astronomy? Technology, scheduling, and coordination can reduce harm, but not eliminate it. How much is acceptable?

6. Is rapid testing responsible? Fast iteration may speed progress and lower cost. It also brings risk to communities and the environment. Where is the right balance?

7. Should wealth drive space? Billionaires have funded many of the biggest advances. Critics worry that private priorities, not public ones, steer the future.

8. Who benefits from space? Satellite internet, weather forecasting, and navigation benefit billions. Tourism benefits the wealthy. How should benefits be shared?

9. Do we have a duty to protect other worlds? Planetary protection rules aim to avoid contamination. Some argue for stricter rules, others for accepting risk in order to explore.

10. Is a multiplanetary future a good idea? Supporters say it is humanity's best insurance. Critics say that it distracts from fixing Earth. Many say we should do both.

How to Argue Well 1. State the other side's view so well that they would agree you got it right. 2. Separate facts from values. 3. Ask what evidence would change your mind. 4. Notice when you are being rewarded for cheering, not thinking.

The Moon and Mars as Science Targets The Moon The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's diameter and has one sixth of its surface gravity. It has almost no atmosphere, temperatures that swing from about 120 degrees Celsius in sunlight to minus 170 at night, and a day that lasts about 29.5 Earth days. A trip takes about three days. Why Go Back? ◆ Science. The Moon holds a record of the early solar system, since it has not

been reshaped by weather or plate tectonics. ◆ Water ice. Permanently shadowed craters near the poles hold ice, confirmed

by several missions. Ice can supply drinking water, oxygen, and rocket propellant. ◆ Testing. The Moon is a nearby place to practice technologies needed for

Mars. ◆ Strategy. Several nations are racing to establish presence and set norms.

Artemis Landing Sites

NASA's candidate sites lie near the south pole, where sunlight is nearly constant on some high ridges and ice may be nearby. These regions are rugged, with long shadows, making landing demanding. Other Landers

Private landers have attempted the Moon with mixed results. Japan's ispace attempts failed in 2023 and 2025. Intuitive Machines' Odysseus landed in February 2024, the first U.S. landing since Apollo 17, but tipped over on landing. Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost landed upright in March 2025. These attempts show how difficult a soft landing is, and why a very large, stable vehicle like Starship has appeal.

Mars Mars has been visited by orbiters, landers, and rovers for half a century. The Viking landers in 1976 searched for life. Sojourner in 1997, Spirit and Opportunity in 2004, Curiosity in 2012, and Perseverance in 2021 each found evidence of ancient water. Perseverance is collecting samples for return to Earth by a future mission, a plan that has been delayed and reshaped by budget issues. Key Scientific Questions ◆ Did life ever exist on Mars? ◆ Where did the water go? ◆ Could humans live there, and for how long? ◆ What does Mars tell us about the history of Earth-like planets?

Landing on Mars

NASA's rovers have used a "sky crane" and heat shields with parachutes and rockets. The biggest landing so far, Curiosity and Perseverance, weigh about one ton. Starship plans to land a vehicle weighing over a hundred tons. That is more than a hundred times larger, and no one has done anything like that on Mars. Engineers must handle retropropulsion, the use of rocket engines for deceleration through a supersonic airstream, which has been studied in Starship's and Falcon's Earth-based tests but not yet proven at Mars. Planetary Protection

International agreements ask spacefaring nations to avoid contaminating other worlds and Earth. Scientists want to find out if life exists on Mars before humans arrive with microbes. This is a serious scientific argument for caution and for thoughtful sequencing of robotic and human missions.

Space Law, Ethics, and the Environment The Outer Space Treaty The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, signed by most spacefaring nations, is the base of international space law. Its principal ideas: ◆ Space is open to all for peaceful use and exploration. ◆ No nation can claim sovereignty over the Moon or other celestial bodies. ◆ Nations are responsible for their national activities, including those of private

companies, and must authorize and supervise them. ◆ No nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. ◆ Nations are liable for damage caused by their space objects.

Later Agreements The Rescue Agreement (1968) requires help for astronauts in distress. The Liability Convention (1972) sets rules for compensation, and the Registration Convention (1975) requires nations to register objects. The Moon Agreement (1979) tried to treat lunar resources as a common heritage but was ratified by few nations, including none of the major spacefaring ones.

The Artemis Accords In 2020, the United States and seven other nations signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for civil exploration, including transparency, interoperability, and "safety zones" around operations. Dozens of countries have since signed. Critics, including Russia and China, argue that the Accords go outside the UN process. Supporters say they create practical norms.

Who Owns Space Resources? The Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 in the United States says that citizens can own resources they extract from asteroids and other bodies, though not the bodies themselves. Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, and Japan passed similar laws. Whether this fits the Outer Space Treaty is argued by lawyers. The comparison often made is to the high seas: a ship does not own the ocean but owns its fish.

Ethical Questions ◆ Planetary protection. Do we have a duty to avoid disturbing possible alien

life, even microbes? ◆ Equity. Who benefits from space wealth? Will poorer nations share in it? ◆ Militarization. Where is the line between defense and weapons in orbit? ◆ Light and sky. Is there a right to a natural night sky? ◆ Safety of participants. How much risk should private passengers or settlers

accept, and who decides?

Environmental Questions Launch Emissions

A rocket's emissions are small compared to aviation or shipping as a whole. A single Falcon 9 launch burns a few hundred tons of kerosene and releases carbon dioxide and water vapor, along with soot in the upper atmosphere. As launch rates grow into the hundreds per year, scientists have asked about stratospheric effects of soot and alumina, and about ozone. Reentry

When satellites burn up, they create aluminum oxides and other particles. Early studies suggest that the quantity could rise sharply with large constellations. The long-term effect is not well understood. Ground Impact

Launch sites affect land, water, and wildlife. Debris from failed launches has fallen in the Gulf of Mexico, and in 2025 pieces of a Starship that failed over the Caribbean disrupted air traffic and landed on islands. The FAA has opened mishap investigations and required changes after such events. Sustainability Measures

Operators propose reusable rockets, cleaner fuels, and responsible disposal of satellites. Methane fuel emits carbon dioxide when burned, but produces less soot than kerosene.

A Framework for Judging When you see a claim about space and the environment, ask: 1. Compared to what? Per launch, per passenger, per satellite, or per year? 2. Is it local or global?
3. Is it reversible? 4. What does independent research say? 5. Who is paying for the measurement?

Futures: Four Scenarios for the 2030s Nobody knows what comes next. A useful way to think about uncertainty is to imagine several plausible futures and ask what would have to be true for each. These four are exercises, not predictions.

Scenario One: The Breakthrough Starship becomes reliable and fully reusable by the end of the decade. Launch prices fall by a factor of ten or more per kilogram. Orbital refueling works. Commercial stations replace the old one, large satellites are launched cheaply, and a crewed Moon landing occurs on or near schedule. Mars cargo flights begin. Costs fall, new businesses appear, and competitors follow with reusable rockets of their own. What would have to be true: heat shield reuse without major repair, rapid turnaround, refueling at scale, regulatory approvals matching flight rates, and demand for the capacity.

Scenario Two: The Long Slog Starship flies often but reuse proves harder than hoped. Refurbishment costs more than planned, and the vehicle's economics are good but not transformational. Falcon 9 stays the workhorse into the 2030s. The Moon landing slips to the end of

the decade or beyond. Mars is a goal for the 2040s. What would have to be true: persistent technical problems at the margin, and cost savings real but modest.

Scenario Three: The Crowded Field Several reusable rockets, from Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, China, and others, enter service. Prices fall because of competition. SpaceX remains the biggest launcher but its share declines. Many constellations fill low orbit, forcing new traffic rules and coordination. Astronomers and regulators negotiate limits. What would have to be true: competitors execute on schedule, and governments choose to diversify.

Scenario Four: The Shock A major accident, a collision cascade, a serious solar storm, a political crisis, or a loss of confidence disrupts the sector. A crewed mission fails, or an orbital collision creates a debris cloud, and regulators pause activities. Investment retreats. The sector recovers more slowly, with stricter safety rules. What would have to be true: a rare but plausible event, such as the ones that reshaped the Shuttle program.

The record keeps rising, so look up the current mark. Why does Falcon 9 land on a ship? For missions that need most of the rocket's performance, the booster travels too far downrange to return to land, so a ship waits in the ocean.

Does a landed booster fly right away? Boosters are inspected and refurbished. About People in Space Has Dragon had any accidents with astronauts aboard? As of this writing, Crew Dragon missions have returned their crews safely.
